newsitem.title: JAPAN: Review shows Japan nuclear agenda on the ropes.
newsitem.headline: Review shows Japan nuclear agenda on the ropes.

text.p: Japan's six-billion dollar Monju prototype fast-breeder nuclear reactor was once considered the crown jewel of this island nation's bold plan to fill its burgeoning energy needs with homegrown technologies.
Now the troubled plant may be headed for the chopping block, a victim of past accidents and a drive to cut government spending.
Government officials said on Wednesday the plant is one of several large-scale public projects due to be reviewed by a government panel for possible elimination.

Located on the Sea of Japan coast in Fukui Prefecture, the 280,000 kilowatt reactor was designed to burn plutonium refined from the spent fuel of conventional reactors, a process thought to be the most promising panacea for a country whose limited natural resources force it to import nearly 100 percent of its oil and gas needs.
But an accident involving the leakage of an estimated two to three tonnes of liquid sodium from a cooling system forced a manual shutdown of the Monju plant in December 1995.
Dormant ever since, the plant now sits at the heart of a debate that could spur Japan to completely re-think the role of nuclear power in its energy mix.
An official at the Science and Technology Agency, which oversees the project, said that a government panel planned to review large-scale projects, including Monju.
He said, however, that he was unaware that any consideration would be given to scrapping the project.
"It's true that Monju is included as one of the projects that will be reviewed...but I haven't heard that the discussion will include abolishing the reactor," the official said.
The Japanese financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported on Wednesday that the government panel would call for drastically scaling down the project if it could not be scrapped.

The Monju accident dealt the first blow to public confidence in the nation's nuclear policy and since then a litany of additional accidents and failed cover-ups has placed Japan's state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Development Corp (PNC) and its nuclear policy under intense public scrutiny.
The government aims to raise the share of nuclear power to 42 percent of total Japanese electricity demand by 2010 from about 34 percent at present.

In March, a PNC-run nuclear fuel reprocessing plant in Tokaimura on the Pacific coast was the scene of Japan's worst-ever nuclear accident when an explosion exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.
Later it was revealed that the chief investigator of Japan's top nuclear agency deliberately destroyed photographs of the accident.
The fall-out of this latest scandal has some analysts convinced Japan's nuclear energy policy has lost its sense of direction.

"The prospect of closing Monju shows the extent to which Japan is off-track in its nuclear development plans," said Alan Troner, Managing Director of the Kuala Lumpur-based consultancy Asia Pacific Energy.
He said part of the problem is that Japan has been running for the last decade with nuclear development projections that are not always based on economic rationale.
"Non-economic, political considerations have played a big role, which means projects are planned and their timetables are continually pushed back," Troner said.

The Nihon Keizai said scrapping Monju would save the nation at least an average 20 billion yen ($160 million) a year, roughly the cost of maintenance and checks on the reactor even when it is not operating.
